stimulus.title: Humanities: Saving Everyday Writing
stimulus.text:
When historians want to know what ordinary people thought and felt in the past, they often turn to letters. Official documents record what governments decided; newspapers record what editors judged worth printing. Letters record something more intimate: the worries of a farmer writing to a brother in the city, the excitement of a young woman describing her first train journey, the small jokes and complaints that make up most of a life.

The value of letters comes partly from their abundance. In the nineteenth century, cheap postage and rising literacy turned letter writing into a habit for millions of people, and families saved what they received. Letters were tied in ribbon, tucked into Bibles, packed into trunks that passed from one generation to the next. Many were lost, of course, but enough survived that archives today hold enormous collections written by people who never imagined anyone but the recipient would read them.

That lack of self-consciousness is precious. A writer who expects publication chooses words carefully and presents a polished self. A writer dashing off a note to a sister about a sick cow or a quarrel with a neighbor does neither. Spelling and grammar, too, can reveal where a writer grew up and how much schooling he or she received. Letters also preserve the texture of their moment in physical ways: the quality of the paper, the handwriting that grows shaky in old age, the stain of a coffee cup, the pressed flower that falls out when the envelope is opened.

I sometimes worry that future historians will have nothing comparable. People today write more than ever, but much of what they write is brief, scattered across many services, and easily deleted. No one ties a bundle of text messages in ribbon. Perhaps some of today's messages will survive by accident, as many old letters did. But accident is a poor archivist. When I imagine a historian a century from now trying to understand how an ordinary family lived in our time, I picture her searching for a trunk that no one thought to fill.
stimulus.text_b:
It is common to hear that our era will leave behind a “digital dark age,” a gap in the historical record caused by fragile files and forgotten passwords. The worry is understandable, and it is not baseless. Storage formats become obsolete, companies shut down their services, and data that is not actively maintained can become unreadable within a few decades. Anyone who has tried to open an old document created with software that no longer exists knows the feeling.

But the fear of a dark age often rests on a romantic picture of the past. The letters that survive from earlier centuries are not a representative sample of what people wrote. They are the ones that happened to be saved, disproportionately by literate, settled, relatively prosperous families with attics to store them in. Countless letters by the poor, the mobile, and the unlucky were burned, thrown out, or left to rot. The archive we inherited was shaped by chance and by privilege as much as by anyone's design.

The digital record, by contrast, is in danger of being too large rather than too small. Ordinary people now produce staggering quantities of writing, and much of it is stored, at least for a time, on servers that keep far more than any attic could hold. The challenge for archivists is not mainly that this material will vanish on its own but that no one will make deliberate decisions about what to keep, in what formats, and with what protections for the privacy of the people who wrote it.

Those decisions are already being made in libraries and archives around the world, where specialists collect websites, preserve email collections donated by writers and organizations, and move files to new formats before the old ones fail. The work is unglamorous and underfunded. Yet it suggests that the historical record of our time will depend less on luck than the record of earlier times did, provided that we are willing to pay for the effort and to argue openly about what deserves to be saved.

Anyone who has tried to open an old document created with software that no longer exists knows the feeling.

But the fear of a dark age often rests on a romantic picture of the past. The letters that survive from earlier centuries are not a representative sample of what people wrote. They are the ones that happened to be saved, disproportionately by literate, settled, relatively prosperous families with attics to store them in. Countless letters by the poor, the mobile, and the unlucky were burned, thrown out, or left to rot. The archive we inherited was shaped by chance and by privilege as much as by anyone's design.

The digital record, by contrast, is in danger of being too large rather than too small. Ordinary people now produce staggering quantities of writing, and much of it is stored, at least for a time, on servers that keep far more than any attic could hold. The challenge for archivists is not mainly that this material will vanish on its own but that no one will make deliberate decisions about what to keep, in what formats, and with what protections for the privacy of the people who wrote it.

Those decisions are already being made in libraries and archives around the world, where specialists collect websites, preserve email collections donated by writers and organizations, and move files to new formats before the old ones fail. The work is unglamorous and underfunded. Yet it suggests that the historical record of our time will depend less on luck than the record of earlier times did, provided that we are willing to pay for the effort and to argue openly about what deserves to be saved.

stimulus.title: Humanities: Saving Everyday Writing
stimulus.text:
When historians want to know what ordinary people thought and felt in the past, they often turn to letters. Official documents record what governments decided; newspapers record what editors judged worth printing. Letters record something more intimate: the worries of a farmer writing to a brother in the city, the excitement of a young woman describing her first train journey, the small jokes and complaints that make up most of a life.

The value of letters comes partly from their abundance. In the nineteenth century, cheap postage and rising literacy turned letter writing into a habit for millions of people, and families saved what they received. Letters were tied in ribbon, tucked into Bibles, packed into trunks that passed from one generation to the next. Many were lost, of course, but enough survived that archives today hold enormous collections written by people who never imagined anyone but the recipient would read them.

That lack of self-consciousness is precious. A writer who expects publication chooses words carefully and presents a polished self. A writer dashing off a note to a sister about a sick cow or a quarrel with a neighbor does neither. Spelling and grammar, too, can reveal where a writer grew up and how much schooling he or she received. Letters also preserve the texture of their moment in physical ways: the quality of the paper, the handwriting that grows shaky in old age, the stain of a coffee cup, the pressed flower that falls out when the envelope is opened.

I sometimes worry that future historians will have nothing comparable. People today write more than ever, but much of what they write is brief, scattered across many services, and easily deleted. No one ties a bundle of text messages in ribbon. Perhaps some of today's messages will survive by accident, as many old letters did. But accident is a poor archivist. When I imagine a historian a century from now trying to understand how an ordinary family lived in our time, I picture her searching for a trunk that no one thought to fill.
